step4.objective:
• An AWP device running RSTP forms a single loop-free active topology with third-party or legacy devices running STP (802.1D) on the same LAN, with exactly one Root Bridge elected across the mixed-protocol network.
  • An AWP device running RSTP interoperates with devices running MSTP, with the MSTP region's CIST parameters and the RSTP device's parameters resolving to one consistent CIST active topology.
  • An AWP device running MSTP interoperates with devices running STP, presenting the region as a single virtual bridge to the STP device and blocking all but one path.
  • Per-port protocol migration is automatic: a port receiving STP Config or TCN BPDUs falls back to sending STP-compatible BPDUs on that port alone, while other ports continue sending RST/MST BPDUs.
  • A port that has fallen back to STP-compatible operation returns to RSTP/MSTP operation after the legacy device stops sending STP BPDUs and the migration delay period elapses.
  • An administrative re-check of the appropriate BPDU type on a port (management-initiated migration check) causes that port to resume transmitting its configured protocol version's BPDUs and to re-detect the peer's protocol.
  • The configured force-protocol-version setting is authoritative: STP-compatible BPDUs and timer values on all ports when set to STP, RST BPDUs when set to RSTP, and full MSTP behaviour when set to MSTP.
  • With force-protocol-version set to STP, rapid transitions are unavailable — a Root Port and an Edge Port each reach Forwarding only via the timer-based Listening and Learning progression, not by rapid transition.
  • A port operating in STP-compatible mode does not use the RSTP proposal/agreement handshake and does not send or act on topology-change notifications in the rapid form.
  • MSTP-to-RSTP boundary ports convey the full CIST information required for the RSTP neighbour to compute a consistent topology, without requiring the RSTP neighbour to be explicitly detected as such.
  • RSTP timer defaults, ranges and semantics conform to 802.1D-2004 (hello time, forward delay, max age, transmit hold count, migration delay), and the values in effect on a port match the operating protocol version on that port.
  • Timer values learned from the Root Bridge are used by non-root devices in the mixed-protocol topology, rather than each device's locally configured values.
  • Bridge and port priority, path cost and root/backup path selection produce the same intended topology regardless of which protocol version each participating device runs.
  • Disconnecting an active link in a mixed STP/RSTP/MSTP topology results in reconvergence to a loop-free topology, with an alternate or backup path taking over.
  • Reconnecting a previously disconnected link results in reconvergence without a loop, without persistent flooding, and without leaving two ports forwarding on the same segment.
  • Repeated disconnect/reconnect cycles on the same and on different links leave the topology stable and consistent, with no stuck port states and no residual blocking of the intended forwarding path.
  • Reconvergence times after link loss and link restoration are consistent with the operating protocol on the affected ports — rapid where RSTP/MSTP applies end-to-end, timer-bound where a segment has fallen back to STP.
  • End-to-end data forwarding is restored across the mixed-protocol topology after each convergence event, and no traffic loops or duplicate frames are observed during or after convergence.
  • MAC address table entries are flushed or aged appropriately on topology change so that forwarding follows the new active topology.
  • Per-port operational state is observable and reports role, state, and the protocol version actually in use on that port, distinguishing configured version from migrated/operating version.
  • Neighbour and peer information is observable per port, including the detected peer protocol type and the elected Root Bridge identifier and root path cost.
  • Spanning-tree statistics and counters are observable per port, including BPDUs transmitted and received by type (Config/TCN/RST/MST) and topology-change counts.
  • Diagnostic and debug output for spanning tree can be enabled and disabled at a selectable level of detail, and reports protocol events including BPDU reception and transmission, migration between protocol versions, role and state transitions, timer expiry and root changes.
  • Debug output identifies the port, protocol version and event for each logged item and does not disrupt protocol operation or convergence when enabled under load.
  • Log and event records are generated for significant topology events — root change, port role or state change, protocol-version migration, and link loss or restoration.
  • Invalid, malformed or out-of-range BPDUs from an interoperating device are discarded without destabilising the local protocol instance, and are counted or reported as errors.
  • Unsupported or out-of-range configuration values for protocol version, timers and priorities are rejected with a clear indication, and previously working values remain in effect.
  • Inconsistent timer configuration that would violate 802.1D-2004 relationships is rejected or reported, rather than silently producing an unstable topology.
  • Configured protocol version, timers, port roles-affecting parameters and debug settings persist across a device restart, and the mixed-protocol topology reconverges to the same intended active topology after restart of any participating device.
  • Behaviour is consistent across shared-media and point-to-point segments, and across an edge port and a non-edge port, when a legacy STP device is present on the segment.

Set up a mixed-protocol LAN containing an AWP device configured for RSTP and a third-party or legacy device running STP (802.1D), with a physically redundant path between them.
Verify that the mixed RSTP/STP network converges to a single loop-free active topology with exactly one Root Bridge elected across all participating devices.
steps.expectedResult: One Root Bridge; all other devices report the same Root Bridge identifier.

steps.description: Confirm that every redundant path in the mixed RSTP/STP topology has exactly one port in a blocking (Discarding/Alternate) role, leaving no loop.
Test with an AWP device running RSTP connected to a device running MSTP, and verify the MSTP region's CIST parameters and the RSTP device's parameters resolve to one consistent CIST active topology.
Verify that both the RSTP device and the MSTP region agree on the CIST Root Bridge identifier and CIST root path cost.
Test with an AWP device running MSTP connected to a device running STP, and verify the MSTP region is presented to the STP device as a single virtual bridge.
Confirm that in the MSTP-to-STP topology all but one path to the STP device is blocked.
Verify per-port automatic protocol migration: send STP Config BPDUs to one port of an RSTP-configured device and confirm that port falls back to transmitting STP-compatible BPDUs.
Repeat the migration check using STP TCN BPDUs instead of Config BPDUs and confirm the same per-port fallback occurs.
Confirm that while one port has fallen back to STP-compatible operation, all other ports on the same device continue transmitting RST or MST BPDUs unchanged.
steps.expectedResult: Fallback is scoped to the receiving port only.

Verify that after the management-initiated migration check the port re-detects the peer's protocol and settles on the correct operating version for that peer.

Verify that MAC address table entries are flushed or aged appropriately on topology change so that forwarding follows the new active topology.
Verify per-port operational state is observable and reports port role and port state on each participating device.
Confirm the per-port output reports the protocol version actually in use on that port and distinguishes the configured version from the migrated/operating version.
Verify neighbour and peer information is observable per port, including the detected peer protocol type.
